question: Should Christians be concerned with material things?
summary: Matthew 6:31, 34 has Jesus instruct disciples to take no thought (*mē merimnēsēte*) for food, drink, clothing, or the morrow. 1 Timothy 5:8 then says if anyone *tōn idiōn kai malista oikeiōn ou pronoei, tēn pistin ērnētai* — 'does not provide for his own, especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.' One text forbids material anxiety; the other makes material provision a test of authentic faith.

reconcile.connective: Gill reads Jesus's ban on anxious "thought for the morrow" as compatible with the ordinary, lawful diligence Paul later commands for one's household.

discrepancy.connective: Sociologist Gerd Theissen's "wandering charismatics" thesis treats the Synoptic ethic of no household provision and the Pastorals' demand to provide for one's own as artifacts of two different, unreconciled stages of the earliest Jesus movement.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874), "Improvidence" (Ethical Discrepancies, p. 281)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pairing directly, quoting Matthew 6:19, 25, 34 and 1 Timothy 5:8 side by side under the heading "Improvidence" and glossing "take no thought" as anxious solicitude, not a ban on ordinary economy or provision (verified via full-text search of the archive.org djvu text).

link.title: What does the Bible say about stress?
link.note: live apologetic treatment citing Matthew 6:25 and 1 Timothy 5:8 together, arguing that family provision is a legitimate responsibility to be pursued in trust rather than anxiety

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: …for it is lawful to take proper care and thought for present food, drink, and raiment; but not to be anxiously concerned for futurity …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill explicitly distinguishes lawful, ordinary care/provision from anxious worry about the future, which is precisely the distinction apologists use to reconcile Jesus's "take no thought" with 1 Timothy 5:8's command to provide for one's household.
